content_preview.title: OpenAI Will Watermark ChatGPT and Codex Text in the EU to Meet AI Act Rules, With an Off-by-Default Option for API Developers Worldwide
content_preview.summary: OpenAI says it will add invisible watermarks to ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU, and API developers anywhere can opt in; testing shows light synonym edits cut detection.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

OpenAI has announced that it will add invisible watermarks to text generated by ChatGPT and Codex in the European Union, according to [TechCrunch](https://techcrunch.com/2026/10/05/openai-will-start-watermarking-chatgpts-text-in-the-eu/). The company is doing so to comply with the EU AI Act's transparency rules. For software teams, the notable detail is that the feature is also available to API developers outside Europe as an opt-in.

editor_notes.content_quality: Clear Briefing structure (Overview, What We Know, Regulatory Background, Comparison, What We Don't Know, Analysis). 628 words, inside the Briefing range of 300-800. Title is 135 characters, under the 150 cap. No quote marks are used in the body; all material is paraphrased and attributed.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all three snapshots from disk (gunzip + text extraction); manifest shows status 200 for all, no archive fallback, suspicious_patterns null for all three, so no injection check was triggered. (1) source-0.html.gz, TechCrunch 5 Oct 2026 (Monday): confirms OpenAI will add an invisible watermark to ChatGPT and Codex text in the EU to comply with the AI Act; rollout over the coming weeks to eligible users on all plans, EU only; API developers anywhere can turn it on for select models starting today and it is off by default; OpenAI is not making it a global default at launch; method called textGrain, shapes word choices, travels with copy/paste; does not identify the user; no meaningful performance change; test of replacing 10% of words with synonyms dropped detection from about 92% to 66%; short passages, math answers and translated text harder to detect; detector access initially limited to approved researchers and expert organizations; missing watermark does not prove human authorship; says Anthropic's watermarking is applied worldwide. Every OpenAI fact in the article is attributed to TechCrunch (OpenAI's own page returned 403 for the writer) and the What We Don't Know section discloses that the OpenAI page could not be retrieved and the supported API model list is unconfirmed. (2) source-1.html.gz, TechCrunch 11 Aug 2026: confirms Anthropic watermarking for text from Claude to comply with European rules; all models released after 2 Aug get it automatically, C2PA for files, support to be extended to older models, applies to Claude platform API, Claude, Claude Code, Claude Cowork and Claude Tag; the support-page statement that the watermark travels with copied text and may persist through some editing; TechCrunch says it is unclear how much editing removes it. The article's Anthropic paragraph matches, and the Anthropic claims were checked against the snapshot rather than credited on trust. Minor wording: article says Anthropic would apply the watermark to models released after August 2 and 'extend the approach to older models', consistent with the source. (3) source-2.html.gz, European Commission digital-strategy page: confirms Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026, providers must add machine-readable marks to enable detection of AI-generated or manipulated content, and that providers that decide not to adhere to the Code of Practice on Transparency of AI-generated Content must demonstrate compliance with marking/labelling obligations through alternative equivalently adequate means. The page does not use the word 'voluntary' for the Code (it says providers 'decide not to adhere'), so 'voluntary' is a light inference, accurate in substance but not literal; info-level only. The page does not mention OpenAI, and the article does not claim it does. The article does not overstate: it says OpenAI is doing this 'to comply' per TechCrunch, and does not assert regulators have approved textGrain (the article explicitly says that is unknown).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: All specifics (92% to 66%, 10% synonyms, textGrain, all plans, EU-only default, worldwide API opt-in off by default, researcher-only detector, C2PA, product list) trace to the snapshots. EU versus worldwide scope and the off-by-default API opt-in are correctly characterised. One inference: 'whereas OpenAI's default rollout is limited to the EU' is supported by source-0. Internal cross-reference /article/2026-08/02-eu-ai-act-transparency-rules-take-effect-requiring-deepfake-and-ai-content-labeling-across-the-bloc uses the correct singular form and resolves to a published article on Article 50 taking effect.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral. Vendor claims attributed to TechCrunch/OpenAI/Anthropic. The Analysis paragraph is restrained and grounded in reported figures. No AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: No existing coverage of OpenAI text watermarking or of Anthropic's August watermarking; the only related article is the August Article 50 explainer, which the new piece links to rather than duplicates. New angle.
concerns: Freshness: TechCrunch OpenAI report is dated 5 Oct 2026, three days before submission; the Anthropic report is from 11 Aug 2026 and is presented as August background, which is acceptable.
OpenAI facts rest solely on a secondary source because OpenAI's page returned 403; handled transparently in the article.
Info: 'voluntary Code of Practice' is a light characterisation not literally on the Commission page.
recommendations: Where a primary vendor page is unreachable, consider an Archive.org copy to confirm the supported-model list.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, properly attributed, correctly scoped and within word and title limits. All domains (techcrunch.com, digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu) are already on the source allowlist; no allowlist changes needed. APPROVE.
